1:
The wise woman who builds her house is first a question of grammar. Charles Ellicott renders it that the wisdom of women builds for each her house while their folly plucks it down, taking both nouns as abstracts. Keil and Delitzsch argue the same case against the received rendering: if the wise among women were meant, why not the plain phrase used elsewhere, and why the individualising verb that follows; the abstract folly in the second half suggests a like abstract in the first, and though one scholar treats the word as an adjective the usage does not bear it. Matthew Henry passes to the thing itself, that a family is multiplied by a fruitful wife and made to prosper by a prudent one, so that debts are paid and children educated and the house has comfort within doors and credit without; she looks on it as her own to care for, though she knows it is her husband’s to bear rule in; and many a family is ruined by ill housewifery. Adam Clarke makes the building material, an increase of property and food, and the pulling down the dilapidation of a thriftless house whose people are ill-fed and worse educated. John Gill takes Wisdom for Christ, who in this book bears that name and builds his house upon himself.

Two of the next verses are turned round. Ellicott reverses the second, so that it reads not that the upright walker fears the Lord but that he who fears the Lord walks in his uprightness. Henry keeps the received order and draws from it that sin reigning is a contempt of God, since those who will not be ruled by his precepts nor accept his promises despise God himself. At the rod of pride Keil and Delitzsch work on a word that occurs elsewhere only once, meaning a brandishing and so a young elastic twig or switch; they report two renderings of an earlier translator, that fools speak tyrannically and that the fool has the sceptre of pride, and object that a sceptre would have required the usual Hebrew word. Henry makes the rod a branch from the root of bitterness in the heart, so that the proud man lays about him with his tongue and it becomes a rod for his own back, as John Wesley also says. Ellicott allows both senses, that the fool smarts for his sayings or punishes others with them; Clarke keeps to the manner of such reproofs, ill-judged and ill-timed and conveyed in language that irritates.

The empty crib produces the fullest note here, a defence of the ox. Clarke sets him against the horse point by point: he is longer lived, scarcely liable to disease, steady and always pulling fair in his gears, able to fatten on what a horse will not eat and so kept at a third of the cost, more profitable in his manure, and when worn out his flesh feeds men, his horns are of great utility and his hide almost invaluable; and costs little in shoeing. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a commendation of cattle-breeding carrying an admonition, to treat gently and repay thankfully the ox God has subjected to man, and more generally to adopt the right means for whatever object one seeks. Ellicott allows two senses, an exhortation to kindness towards animals or an observation that labour has its disagreeable side and its reward. Henry finds the joke in the cleanness: the crib is clean of dung, which pleases the nice, who cannot endure husbandry for its dirty work and will sell their oxen to keep it clean, though the dung of the ox is wanted as well as his labour. Gill notes that the word for clean is elsewhere used for wheat, so the line may mean the granary is without corn; Wesley recalls that cleanness of teeth stands elsewhere for famine.
7:
The seventh verse tells a man to leave a fool. John Gill reads it plainly: shun his company, the thing being dangerous and infectious. Keil and Delitzsch render the second half as and surely thou hast not known lips of knowledge, denying that it gives a reason for going, which would have called for a different particle, as two early translators assumed; the noun behind it is the sphere of vision, and the compound marks a distance from that sphere at which the object is still in sight. Matthew Henry makes the clause a test: if we find no relish or savour of piety in a man’s discourse, but only what is corrupt and corrupting, we may conclude the treasure is bad; and sometimes the only way of reproving wicked discourse is by leaving the company. Adam Clarke notes several manuscripts reading a lie where the text has knowledge, and adds that how this reading came he cannot conjecture. Charles Ellicott fixes the departure at the point where you see you can do him no good, and instances Samuel, who came no more to see Saul.

Prudence in the next verse is practical, not speculative. Henry insists it is not the wisdom of the learned but the wisdom that directs our counsels and actions: we are travellers whose concern is to get forward, not to spy wonders. Gill takes the way as that of a man’s calling, duty and salvation, and John Wesley says the wit of ungodly men is employed only in finding out ways of deceiving. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to make the answering folly a self-deceit, though three old versions render it error, because the word is never so used and the notion of malicious fraud clings to it. Ellicott agrees the folly shows itself in cheating others, who are sure to detect it, and Clarke records a manuscript reading direct his way for understand his way.

The ninth verse is where the learned get into trouble, as Clarke says: some by their criticisms have brought it into embarrassments out of which they could not extricate it. Keil and Delitzsch try anyway, reading the sacrificial offering of fools mocketh; they refuse the verb the senses of excusing and of mediating that two interpreters gave it, and take the offering as expiation, a penitential work. Gill reports that some render the word a sin offering, and turns the mockery against those who displace Christ’s offering. Henry sets that reading beside the common one and concludes that those who make light of sin make light of Christ. Ellicott offers both that sin mocks fools, who miss the gratification they expected, and that the sin offering mocks them, unaccepted by God.

Bitterness of soul closes the group. Clarke says that under spiritual sorrow the heart feels and the whole animal nature suffers, and that a stranger to such feelings cannot intermeddle, not understanding them. Gill observes that this is not every heart’s case, since a man may be in the gall of bitterness and feel none of it. Henry warns that we must not censure the griefs of others, whose stroke is perhaps heavier than their groaning, and Wesley keeps the matter shut up in a man’s self. Ellicott names the one exception, the Son of Man who came to bear our griefs yet could join the marriage feast. Then Keil and Delitzsch observe that the apparently firm house is assigned to the wicked while the fragile tent, never set up as though it would last, is assigned to the upright and yet blossoms and shoots; Ellicott sets the contrast the same way, and Henry adds that sin ruins great families while righteousness raises mean ones. On the way that seems right, Keil and Delitzsch call the rightness a phantom of self-deception, Henry concludes that self-deceivers prove self-destroyers, and Clarke recalls persecutors who thought burning others was doing God service.
13:
Sadness inside laughter draws the longest note here. Keil and Delitzsch ground it in the human heart, which carries a disquiet, a sense of separation from its true home and of the transitoriness of earthly things, besides many a secret sorrow; that sorrow cannot be expelled, and returns the more intensely the more it has been kept under. Matthew Henry takes it as proof that carnal mirth is mad: sinners under conviction dissemble their grief by a forced mirth, and the joy of the hypocrite is but from the teeth outward, soon over, like the crackling of thorns under a pot. Adam Clarke keeps to the hard task of a face of mirth over a heavy heart, John Gill instances Belshazzar, merry until the writing on the wall, and Charles Ellicott takes it as God teaching that nothing but himself can satisfy the soul.

The backslider produces Clarke’s most systematic page, questions answered in order. He is the man who once walked in religion and has withdrawn, who once fought manfully and has since joined the enemy, who once belonged to the saints and now sits in the synagogue of Satan; the backslider in heart is not the man surprised by temptation but the man who drinks down iniquity with greediness; and his own ways are folly, sin, disappointment and death. Henry makes the filling an eternal surfeit: they would not leave their lusts, so their lusts shall stick by them. Ellicott says they get what they look for, though it is swine’s husks and not food fit for God’s children, and Keil and Delitzsch define the good man by self-sacrificing love as his motive.

Credulity and caution follow. Keil and Delitzsch will not read the simple man’s belief as belief in every thing, word and faith being correlates; he is not self-dependent, believes without proving whether what he hears is well-meant or true, and is driven hither and thither, while the prudent marks his step. Henry lists the marks of credulity: heeding every flying report, taking things on trust from common fame, crediting every one who will promise payment; the prudent tries before he trusts, weighing the witness and the probability of the testimony. John Wesley adds that he weighs not what others say but what he ought to do. At the wise man who fears, Keil and Delitzsch reject the renderings that make the fool merely over-confident or headlong, the verb meaning everywhere to fall into extreme anger, and define the fear as a self-mistrusting reserve flowing from reverential awe. Clarke pairs caution with confidence, the one leading the wise man from sin and the other to God; Gill makes his motive not fear of punishment, as one rabbi held, but a sense of goodness.

The last two verses set the hasty man beside the cold one. Clarke explains the Hebrew for soon angry as short of nostrils, since anger contracts the nose and draws it towards the eyes; such a man has no time for reflection. Henry finds him pitiable, the fit being soon over and he sorry for it, while the man of wicked devices, who stifles his resentment till he has opportunity of revenge, is odious and there is no fence against him; Ellicott makes him an object of ridicule but not of hatred. Keil and Delitzsch report that Ewald found no right contrast here and corrected the text so that the man of consideration smooths his soul; they answer that the phrase need not be taken in a good sense and the received text is good Hebrew. On the last verse they labour over the crowning word, canvassing an Arabic root for abundance, a sense of waiting behind two ancient renderings, and a sense of encompassing, each too weak for the case. Henry and Gill make the folly hereditary, held as fast as an estate; Ellicott compares weeds in unoccupied soil.
19:
The evil bowing before the good is read as present sight and as distant promise. Keil and Delitzsch take the good as that which has love for its principle and must at last hold the supremacy, so that men fall from prosperity far enough to post themselves at the entrance of the stately dwelling, waiting for him to go out and in. Adam Clarke keeps it immediate: those who have wasted their substance beg bread at the gates of benevolent men. Matthew Henry allows that, adding that good men give even to the evil, since where God grants life we must not deny a livelihood, and looking on to the day when foolish virgins beg oil of the wise. John Gill reports a rabbi who referred the whole to a future glory and finds only scattered instances, Haman before Mordecai and heathen emperors before Constantine; Charles Ellicott rests the certainty of the retribution on the tense.

The poor man hated by his neighbour is offered as a fact of the world, not a rule of duty. Keil and Delitzsch call it the old history daily repeating itself, a part of the dark side of human nature, so that a man in prosperity may not think all his friends genuine and in poverty may value the exceptions the higher; they quote a Latin poet on the happy man who counts many friends and the clouded man who sits alone. Clarke quotes the same lines and adds another comparison, that false friends are swallows, gone when the cold drives them off; Henry has the figure in English, most being swallow-friends, gone in winter; God, he adds, will not desert us when we are poor. Gill observes that the same man is respected or slighted as he stands in affluence or want.

Contempt for a neighbour raises a question of what the word covers. Keil and Delitzsch deny that it means speaking contemptuously to a man’s face; it is treatment that insults rather than mocks, and no German or English expression completely answers to it. The intelligent man keeps his judgment to himself, abstaining from criticism because he knows he is not infallible nor acquainted with the heart. Clarke makes the injustice concrete: to despise a man for a natural blemish is cruel, since he is not the author of his imperfections and would not retain them if he could. Henry puts the despiser among those who set a neighbour with the dogs of their flock; Gill notes two old versions reading it of the poor. At the deviser of evil, Keil and Delitzsch refuse two emendations of Hitzig, a doubling of the participle to mean plotters and an alteration of the verb, and keep the ploughing sense beside that of fabricating; Gill has the same image, of mischief ploughed and sown in hope of a fine harvest. Henry adds that the justice of God cannot be out-witted.

Labour and talk close the group. Keil and Delitzsch note that a long run of these proverbs is bound by key-words beginning with one letter, and trace the word for gain to a root meaning stretched out long, hence what hangs over and is left above the endeavour. Henry states the pair: working without talking makes men rich, the stirring hand getting a penny, and talking without working makes them poor, the time going in tittle-tattle and hearing new things. Clarke adds that a man of words is seldom a man of deeds. On the crown of the wise, Keil and Delitzsch reject a proposal to read prudence for riches, since riches coming to a man who already has wisdom heighten its influence. Henry says wisdom is good without an inheritance but better with it, Ellicott that a rich fool displays his folly the more from a conspicuous place, and John Wesley that his folly is not cured but made worse by his riches.
25:
The true witness is taken at full weight. Keil and Delitzsch set the scene in a criminal process, where men in danger of their lives through false accusation are saved by a tongue pressed by conscientiousness and not deterred by cowardice; the opposite breathes out lies and is nothing but deception. Matthew Henry adds that the good names of the innocent are as dear as their lives, that a man of integrity will venture the displeasure of the greatest for the truth, and that a nation should punish false witness, since truth is the cement of society. John Gill notes that the delivering is of souls in the plural, a whole family or more, and that an old version adds from evils.

The fear of the Lord gets two verses, and the interest falls on where the strength lies. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to make the fear itself the thing relied on: it has an enduring inheritance in God, for it is not faith nor anything subjective that is the rock bearing us up, but the object which faith lays hold of. Charles Ellicott asks whose children find the refuge, either the children of the man who fears, as such promises descended to the seed, or the children of God who look up to him as a father. Henry takes the first way, since children of religious parents often fare the better for their instruction and example. Adam Clarke notes that the fear of God is highly consistent with the strongest confidence in his mercy, and gives the Hebrew of the fountain of life as the vein of lives, an allusion, he thinks, to the great artery carrying blood to the extremities. Gill hears there the well of living water springing up to everlasting life.

On the multitude of the people the voices go different ways. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the words, giving the root of the honour as swelling or enlarging, and noting that the term opposed to it means elsewhere without or groundless but here denotes ruin. Henry calls it two maxims in politics that carry their own evidence, that a populous kingdom is a sign of good rule since strangers settle under such protection, and that princes should increase their people by mild government and by encouraging trade and husbandry. Ellicott hears the man of rest, and puts the honour here and not in ambitious wars. Clarke turns it into policy of his own: every state should promote marriage, disgrace celibacy, bar bachelors from public employment after a certain age, and banish the religious houses as having contributed more to vice than virtue. Gill reads the crowded kingdom as a sign of clemency and righteousness, liberty and property enjoyed.

The last pair turn on temper. Keil and Delitzsch parse the slow man as one who shuts the outbreak of anger long out, and the hasty as short in spirit, shortness of time being meant. Clarke gives the same phrase as the short of spirit, so agitated as to be short of breath, and sets it against the long of nostrils. Henry makes meekness wisdom, since such a man understands human infirmity and knows how to adjourn his resentments, while the hasty man, all fire and tow, thinks to make others stand in awe and only exalts his folly. Ellicott offers two senses for it, bringing folly into view or carrying it off as his portion, and John Wesley has it lifted like a banner. At the sound heart, Keil and Delitzsch describe the quiet heart as a calm water-mirror, neither interrupted by the affections nor stirred by passion; Henry says people grow fat with good humour while the envious spirit preys on the animal spirits and makes the countenance pale; Clarke reduces it to healthy blood; and Gill prefers a healing heart, humane and friendly, the life of others as well as of its own flesh.
31:
Oppression of the poor is made an affront to God. Matthew Henry presses the reasoning: God made the poor man and appointed him his lot, so that dealing hardly with any because they are poor reflects upon God as having laid them low. Charles Ellicott would render the second line rather that he who has mercy on the poor honours him. Adam Clarke says the poor are in the order of God part of the inhabitants of the earth, given us for the exercise of compassionate feelings without which men had been little better than brutes. John Gill itemises the oppression as scoffing at poverty, vexatious lawsuits, withholding wages or refusing relief; John Wesley says the poor man bears his Maker’s image; and Keil and Delitzsch note that the predicates follow one another in a chiasmus.

The wicked driven away draws a textual quarrel. Keil and Delitzsch render that when misfortune befalls him the godless is overthrown, the righteous remaining hopeful in his death; the old versions, they report, altered the last words to read in his uprightness for the sake of an exact parallelism, and they answer that no word of Scripture commends self-righteousness so contradictorily and that the verb never denotes self-confidence. Ellicott takes the first line the same way, the man overthrown in his misfortune with none to aid or comfort him. Henry keeps the common rendering: the man cleaves so closely to the world that he must be driven out of it, and sin cleaves so closely to him that it goes with him into another world. Gill has him driven as a beast is, sore against his will, where the righteous depart and desire to depart.

Wisdom resting in the heart is the hardest verse. Keil and Delitzsch say most interpreters know not what to make of the second line, and list the attempts: the old versions insert a negative, a paraphrase supplies the word folly, one scholar makes wisdom lost in the heart of fools and another makes it reel about; they call these imaginary and follow the one commentator who adheres to the ascertained meaning. Ellicott reaches the same result without apparatus, wisdom being the subject of both halves: the man of understanding does not care to drag it out, but the fool cannot keep to himself anything he thinks he knows. Henry makes modesty the badge of wisdom, since the wise man digests what he knows without making a noise with it, and wisdom must rest in the heart and not swim in the head, whereas fools take all occasions to bring their little knowledge in by head and shoulders. Gill makes the heart a treasury where wisdom lies undisturbed, and Wesley has fools publishing in all times and companies.

The last two verses turn to the state. Clarke is not satisfied that sin is a reproach to any people, and would render the line that mercy is a sin-offering for them, citing a Latin version in which sin makes a people wretched and a Greek in which sins lessen the tribes; his own sense is that a national disposition to mercy appears before God as a continual sin-offering, atoning for nothing. Keil and Delitzsch spend their note on vocabulary, distinguishing a people as a mass swollen from a common origin, a people confederated under common law, and the multitude. Henry notes that alms are sometimes called righteousness, and that Israel was an instance of both halves, great when good. At the king’s favour Clarke writes the chapter’s most personal note: a king should have a minister of deep sense and merciful disposition, since want of the first plunges the nation into difficulties and want of the second embarks her in disastrous wars, most wars being occasioned by bad ministers, men of blood. Henry adds that in a well-ordered government no man’s services are neglected to please a party or a favourite.
